titles.683: Man. Post. Cap. X: GAR — ‘no imputation without law’ only means knowing willful breach (Rom 4:15 / Calvin)
titles.684: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — I take ‘no law, no imputation’ absolutely; sin is ἀνομία judged by a law
titles.685: Man. Post. Cap. X: GAR — God needs no external law for occult judgment; Canaan / Abimelech cited
titles.686: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — judicial imputation always tracks some law; Canaan case is not universal judgment
titles.687: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — Gen 2:17 does not carve imputation of the bite onto all posterity
titles.688: Man. Post. Cap. X tip — we are punished for Adam’s sin via propagated corruption, not immediately

latin.683: GAR. Responsio in promptu est. Interim enim quod dicit Apostolus, non imputari peccatum ubi non est lex, omnino genuinum est illi quod prius dixerat, Romani IV. 15. Ubi non est lex, ibi nec transgressio est, quod Calvinus, ad quem provocat opponens, ita exponit, ut doceat Apostolum non loqui de simplici ulla transgressione, a qua nemo eximitur, sed transgressionem appellare ubi animus edoctus quid Deo placeat, quidve displiceat, finitis voce Dei sibi definitis, sciens ac volens perrumpit, &c.
latin.684: PLAC. Haec responsio ad rem non est. Propositio enim illa, non imputatur peccatum ubi non est lex, accipitur a Calvino cum restrictione ad legem scriptam, & hominum iudicium. Ego vero illam nunc quidem usurpo absolute & sine restrictione, quatenus, universaliter accepta, vera est. Quid enim est in genere peccatum, nisi ἀνομία, aberratio a lege, legis transgressio? & quid est iudiciaria imputatio, nisi actio iudicis iudicantis secundum legem, sive ea naturalis, sive positiva, voce aut scripto, lata fuerit?
latin.685: GAR. Deo non sunt leges externae constitutae, secundum quas necessario ipsi agendum sit, praesertim in iudiciis occultis. Deus noster in caelo, quodcumque libuerit, facit, Psalmo cxv. 3. Atqui imputatio peccati Adae est actio Dei iudiciaria, ut dicebamus ab initio, in qua occultum iudicium & admirabile consilium eius agnoscendum est. Ergo etiam sine lege posita, potuit illud peccatum imputare. Sic ante legem a Mose traditam, imputatum est Canaanis a Deo Chami patris peccatum, & peccati ab Abimelecho commissi poenas dedit familia. Quis legem externam proferat tunc existentem, secundum cuius regulam ea imputatio facta fuerit?
latin.686: PLAC. Primum de lege in genere agebatur, non in specie de lege externa. Aberrat igitur Vir doctus ab argumento cui respondere se profitetur. Deinde, non quaerebatur, an essent positae leges Deo secundum quas ipsi necessario agendum esset. Hoc plane alienum est a proposito. Tantum contendo omnem imputationem peccati iudiciariam fieri secundum aliquam legem. Quomodo enim actio iudiciaria esse potest, si non sit a iudice, & ut iudicem decet? Iudex autem cum peccatum imputat, cum damnat, cum punit, respectum habet ad legem, ut iustitiae, ut legi satisfiat. Alioqui causam non video, cur eiusmodi actio iudiciaria dicatur. Quod ait imputatum a Deo Canaanis peccatum patris Chami fuisse, id si verum est, imputatio illa non fuit actio iudiciaria; itaque non pertinuit ad omnes Chami posteros; aut si iudiciaria fuit, ex omnibus filiis Chami auctor vel particeps illius culpae solus Canaan fuit. Certe illius solius, etiam patre Chamo omisso, Noachus, cum maledictionem pronunciaret, nomen, & quidem ter, expressit.
latin.687: Quod §. xxviii. sequente subiungit Vir doctus legem secundum quam illa imputatio iudiciaria sit, esse primigeniam illam legem, Quo die comederis, morte morieris, mihi mirum videtur. Quo enim argumento ex verbis illis exsculpsit, manducationem illam omnibus Adami posteris imputari debere? Participes quidem sunt poenarum omnes homines, sed quia sunt participes peccati. Hoc enim propagato, quid est cur illae non propagatae fuissent?
latin.688: Vidit in posteris Adami Deus malitiam omnem inobedientiae Adami, corruptionem haereditariam, hoc est, incredulitatem, inimicitiam habitualem adversus Deum, legi naturae repugnantiam &c., similiter malis similibus poenis addixit. Flagitat enim naturae lex, ut pariter malis, pariter male sit. Punimur ergo propter peccatum Adami, sed mediante corruptione propagata, non immediate sunt illae poenae.

pass_a.683: Garissoles: ready reply. Paul’s ‘sin is not imputed where there is no law’ matches Rom 4:15 (‘where no law, no transgression’). Calvin, whom the opponent cites, takes Paul not of every simple breach none escape, but of willful breach where a mind taught what God likes and dislikes, by God’s defined word, knowingly and willingly breaks through.
pass_a.684: Placeus: that misses the point. Calvin restricts the maxim to written law and human courts. Placeus uses it absolutely and without restriction, as universally true. What is sin in general but ἀνομία—wandering from a law, law-breach? And what is judicial imputation but a judge’s act judging by a law—natural or positive, spoken or written?
pass_a.685: Garissoles: God has no external laws he must follow, especially in occult judgments—our God in heaven does whatever he wills (Ps 115:3). Adam-sin imputation is God’s judicial act with hidden judgment and wondrous counsel; so he could impute without a posited law. Before Moses, God imputed Ham’s sin to Canaan, and Abimelech’s household paid for his sin—what external law then ruled that imputation?
pass_a.686: Placeus: we argued about law in general, not external law in species—so the learned man misses the case. Nor did we ask whether God is bound by laws he must obey. Claim only: every judicial imputation of sin runs by some law. How is an act judicial if not from a judge as a judge should act? When he imputes, damns, punishes, he looks to a law so justice and law are satisfied—else why call it judicial? If Canaan truly bore Ham’s sin, that was not a universal judicial act on all Ham’s line; or if judicial, among Ham’s sons only Canaan shared the guilt—Noah thrice named Canaan alone in the curse, even omitting Ham.
pass_a.687: That the following §28 makes the judicial law the primal ‘in the day you eat you shall die’ amazes Placeus. By what argument do those words carve that the bite must be imputed to all Adam’s posterity? All share the penalties because they share the sin; once the sin is propagated, why would the penalties not be?
pass_a.688: In Adam’s posterity God saw all the malice of Adam’s disobedience—hereditary corruption: unbelief, habitual enmity toward God, clash with nature’s law, etc.—and likewise sentenced like evils with like penalties. Nature’s law demands that like evils fare alike. So we are punished for Adam’s sin, but through propagated corruption; those penalties are not immediate.

683: GAR. The reply is ready at hand.

For meanwhile what the Apostle says—that sin is not imputed where there is no law—is altogether genuine to what he had said earlier in Romans 4:15: Where there is no law, there is no transgression either—which Calvin, to whom the opponent appeals, so explains as to teach that the Apostle is not speaking of any simple transgression from which no one is exempt, but calls it transgression where a mind taught what pleases God and what displeases him, with limits defined for it by God’s voice, knowingly and willingly breaks through, etc.
684: PLAC. This reply is not to the point.
For that proposition, sin is not imputed where there is no law, is taken by Calvin with a restriction to the written law and to men’s judgment.
But I now use it absolutely and without restriction, insofar as, taken universally, it is true.
For what is sin in general but ἀνομία, a wandering from a law, a transgression of law?
And what is judicial imputation but the act of a judge judging according to a law, whether that law was natural or positive, given by voice or in writing?
685: GAR. God has no external laws constituted according to which he must necessarily act, especially in occult judgments.
Our God is in heaven; he does whatever he has pleased (Psalm 115:3).
But the imputation of Adam’s sin is a judicial act of God, as we said from the start, in which his hidden judgment and admirable counsel are to be acknowledged.
Therefore even without a law posited he could impute that sin.
So before the law handed down by Moses, Canaan had Ham the father’s sin imputed by God, and the household paid the penalties of the sin committed by Abimelech.
Who will produce an external law then existing, according to whose rule that imputation was made?
686: PLAC. First, the discussion was about law in general, not in species about an external law.
So the learned man wanders from the argument to which he professes to reply.
Next, it was not asked whether laws had been set for God according to which he must necessarily act.
That is plainly foreign to the purpose.
I contend only that every judicial imputation of sin is made according to some law.
For how can an act be judicial if it is not from a judge, and as befits a judge?
But a judge, when he imputes sin, when he condemns, when he punishes, has respect to a law, that justice may be done, that the law may be satisfied.
Otherwise I do not see why such an act is called judicial.

As for his saying that Ham the father’s sin was imputed by God to Canaan: if that is true, that imputation was not a judicial act; and so it did not reach all Ham’s posterity; or if it was judicial, among all Ham’s sons the author or sharer of that guilt was Canaan alone.
Certainly Noah, when he pronounced the curse, expressed that one’s name alone—and thrice—even omitting father Ham.
687: What the learned man adds in the following §28—that the law according to which that judicial imputation is made is that primal law, In the day you eat you shall die—seems marvelous to me.
For by what argument has he carved out of those words that that eating ought to be imputed to all Adam’s posterity?
All men are indeed sharers in the penalties, but because they are sharers in the sin.
For once this was propagated, what reason is there why those penalties would not have been propagated?
688: In Adam’s posterity God saw all the malice of Adam’s disobedience, hereditary corruption—that is, unbelief, habitual enmity against God, opposition to the law of nature, and the like—and likewise sentenced like evils to like penalties.
For the law of nature demands that it go equally ill with equal evils.
We are therefore punished on account of Adam’s sin, but through the mediation of propagated corruption; those penalties are not immediate.
